summary: Discusses requirements for inter-AS MPLS Traffic Engineering, presenting scenarios and general guidelines for solutions. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4216 explains why network providers may need traffic-engineered paths across autonomous-system borders. It describes those use cases and lists requirements for a possible solution, but it does not define one.

questions: what is inter-as mpls traffic engineering
why is bgp not enough for traffic engineering
subtitle: Requirements for engineering MPLS paths across autonomous-system borders.

tldr.problem: MPLS traffic engineering was defined within one autonomous system, but providers also wanted controlled paths across several systems.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes five use cases and lists requirements for signaling, path computation, recovery, scale, management, confidentiality, and policy.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document. It gives no protocol and makes no claim that a solution can meet every requirement.

facts.label: Main objectives
facts.value: Bandwidth guarantees, resource optimization, fast recovery

today: RFC 4216 is an Informational document published in November 2005. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it records scenarios and requirements, not a protocol.

sections.title: Why Traffic Engineering Crosses Borders
sections.content:
RFC 4216 considers Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) traffic engineering across autonomous systems (ASes). It targets the same objectives as traffic engineering inside one AS: bandwidth guarantees for services, better use of network resources, and fast recovery after failures.

Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) attributes can steer traffic between ASes, but the RFC describes that control as coarse. Its scope is a finer-grained MPLS approach for IP/MPLS networks. It does not claim that a practical solution can satisfy every requirement in the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC asks how providers could control paths that cross network boundaries. It lists needs for that work, but it does not say that every need can be met.

sections.title: Three Goals for Inter-AS Paths
sections.content:
The first goal is an end-to-end bandwidth guarantee. Diffserv can apply quality-of-service policies, but strict bounds may also require admission control inside the network. The RFC uses voice traffic in the Expedited Forwarding class as an example.

The other goals are resource optimization and fast recovery. BGP-based choices may become complex as inter-AS links grow or providers change routing independently. A path must also recover quickly from failures of links, shared-risk link groups, or border routers.
sections.plainLanguage: Providers want paths with reserved capacity, efficient use of links, and quick recovery after failures. The RFC says existing inter-AS routing can make those goals difficult to achieve together.

sections.title: Five Application Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC describes five uses. A provider may extend a point of presence into another provider's region, use a provider's edge router as an extended trunk, or connect customer edge routers across several providers. These first three scenarios chiefly need bandwidth guarantees.

The other scenarios cover traffic engineering across several ASes run by one provider and using transit ASes as primary or backup transport. These chiefly aim to optimize resources. The customer-edge-to-customer-edge case may not scale well as a partial or full mesh unless hierarchical tunnels reduce signaling state.
sections.plainLanguage: The use cases include extending service through another provider and joining networks across several providers. They also include optimizing a provider's own regions or using other networks as transit.

sections.title: Requirements Within One Provider
sections.content:
A solution must interoperate with existing intra-AS MPLS traffic engineering and inherit its capabilities. The RFC calls for end-to-end signaling, explicit or discovered path elements, optional exclusions, optimal or near-optimal paths, diverse paths, and non-disruptive re-optimization. It also calls for fast reroute and differentiated-services-aware traffic engineering.

The solution must limit added load on IGP, BGP, and RSVP-TE. The document also calls for tunnel aggregation, ways to map traffic onto tunnels, management and fault-detection support, extensibility, backward compatibility, and performance evaluation.
sections.plainLanguage: A solution should work with the traffic engineering already used inside a provider. It must also limit extra network state and support path changes, failure recovery, and management.

sections.title: Policy and Security Between Providers
sections.content:
When a path crosses providers, one provider may need to hide its internal hops while still sharing enough information for path computation. Policy at an AS border could enforce agreements, limit requested bandwidth, reject requests, or rewrite request attributes. The RFC also calls for policing traffic against the bandwidth agreed during signaling.

The security section says a solution must address security across provider domains. Providers should be able to authenticate signaling, decide which requests to allow, and protect against denial-of-service attacks. The RFC says a trusted model across AS borders needs particular attention.
sections.plainLanguage: Each provider may need to protect its internal network details and enforce its own rules. Providers also need to authenticate requests and limit traffic to agreed capacity.
